title: [A2 • Band 4.0] Bài 115: The Hydraulic Architecture of Petra
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 115 (LEVEL A2 • BAND 4.0)

The Hydraulic Architecture of Petra

Paragraph 1. Petra is an ancient stone city hidden inside red rock valleys in southern Jordan. Long ago, around twenty thousand people lived there comfortably. The desert around Petra is very dry, getting only 150 millimetres of rain each year. Even so, Petra became very rich because it stood at the centre of busy desert trade routes. Merchants travelled through the city carrying incense, spices, and silk between Arabia, Egypt, and India.

Paragraph 2. Petra had a serious water problem. For most of the year, the land was dry and hot. In winter, however, sudden heavy storms hit the nearby mountains. Fast floodwaters rushed straight down into the narrow valley entrance of the city. To protect travellers and buildings, skilled Nabataean builders erected a tall stone wall across the entrance. They also cut a long tunnel straight through solid rock to guide the dangerous floodwater safely away from the city centre.

Paragraph 3. After stopping the floods, the builders saved rainwater for dry months. They carved open rock channels and laid clay water pipes for many kilometres from mountain springs into Petra. Because the pipes sloped gently downward, water flowed naturally into town using only gravity. Workers joined the clay pipes with special natural lime glue so water would not leak out. Deep underground rooms stored millions of litres of clean water.

Paragraph 4. With plenty of clean water, Petra had public bathhouses, street fountains, and green gardens full of palm trees. Later, Roman rulers took control of the region, and trade ships slowly replaced desert caravans. Finally, in 363 CE, a terrible earthquake broke the underground water pipes and tanks. Without water or money to rebuild, people left Petra, and desert sand slowly covered the city.

steps: Đoạn 3: "Workers joined the clay pipes with special natural lime glue so water would not leak out."
